claim: RNF220 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase widely involved in neural development via targeting of multiple substrates.
source: RNF220, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, is widely involved in neural development via targeting of multiple substrates.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work (Kim et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022c) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Hox genes in the pons were markedly up-regulated at late developmental stages (post-embryonic day E15.5) in Rnf220-/- and Rnf220+/- mouse embryos.
source: Here, we found that the expression of Hox genes in the pons was markedly up-regulated at the late developmental stage (post-embryonic day E15.5) in Rnf220-/- and Rnf220+/- mouse embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from microarray analysis and qRT-PCR as described in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing analysis revealed different Hox de-repression profiles in different groups of neurons, including the pontine nuclei.
source: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis revealed different Hox de-repression profiles in different groups of neurons, including the pontine nuclei (PN).
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data presented in Figure 1B-D showing distinct Hox expression patterns across different cell clusters.

claim: The Hox pattern was disrupted in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice.
source: The Hox pattern was disrupted and the neural circuits were affected in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating altered Hox3-5 expression patterns along the rostral-caudal axis.

claim: Neural circuits were affected in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice.
source: The Hox pattern was disrupted and the neural circuits were affected in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by neuronal tracing data shown in Figure 2C, F-G demonstrating altered projection patterns from motor cortex to PN.

claim: WDR5 is a key component of the TrxG complex.
source: We showed that this phenomenon was mediated by WDR5, a key component of the TrxG complex, which can be polyubiquitinated and degraded by RNF220.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about WDR5's role in the COMPASS/TrxG complex, as referenced in the Introduction (Wysocka et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: WDR5 can be polyubiquitinated and degraded by RNF220.
source: We showed that this phenomenon was mediated by WDR5, a key component of the TrxG complex, which can be polyubiquitinated and degraded by RNF220.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 4A-C), ubiquitination assays (Figure 4F-I), and protein stability assays (Figure 4D-E).

claim: Intrauterine injection of WDR5 inhibitor (WDR5-IN-4) largely recovered the de-repressed Hox expression pattern in the hindbrain of Rnf220+/- mice.
source: Intrauterine injection of WDR5 inhibitor (WDR5-IN-4) and genetic ablation of Wdr5 in Rnf220+/- mice largely recovered the de-repressed Hox expression pattern in the hindbrain.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C demonstrating rescue of Hox gene expression following WDR5-IN-4 treatment.

claim: Genetic ablation of Wdr5 in Rnf220+/- mice largely recovered the de-repressed Hox expression pattern in the hindbrain.
source: Intrauterine injection of WDR5 inhibitor (WDR5-IN-4) and genetic ablation of Wdr5 in Rnf220+/- mice largely recovered the de-repressed Hox expression pattern in the hindbrain.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E demonstrating rescue of Hox gene expression in Rnf220fl/wt;Wdr5fl/wt;Nestin-Cre mice.

claim: In P19 embryonal carcinoma cells, retinoic acid-induced Hox expression was further stimulated by Rnf220 knockdown.
source: In P19 embryonal carcinoma cells, the retinoic acid-induced Hox expression was further stimulated by Rnf220 knockdown, which can also be rescued by Wdr5 knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating enhanced Hox gene expression upon Rnf220 knockdown in RA-treated P19 cells.

claim: The stimulation of Hox expression by Rnf220 knockdown in P19 cells can be rescued by Wdr5 knockdown.
source: In P19 embryonal carcinoma cells, the retinoic acid-induced Hox expression was further stimulated by Rnf220 knockdown, which can also be rescued by Wdr5 knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C demonstrating that Wdr5 knockdown reverses the effect of Rnf220 knockdown on Hox gene expression.

claim: There are 39 Hox genes organized in four clusters (Hoxa, Hoxb, Hoxc, and Hoxd) in mammals.
source: In mammals, there are 39 Hox genes organized in four clusters (Hoxa, Hoxb, Hoxc, and Hoxd) and divided into 1–13 paralog groups (PG).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian Hox gene organization.

claim: Mammalian Hox genes are divided into 1-13 paralog groups.
source: In mammals, there are 39 Hox genes organized in four clusters (Hoxa, Hoxb, Hoxc, and Hoxd) and divided into 1–13 paralog groups (PG).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian Hox gene organization.

claim: The vertebrate hindbrain forms eight metameric segmented units along the antero-posterior axis known as rhombomeres.
source: During vertebrate development, the hindbrain forms eight metameric segmented units along the antero-posterior (A-P) axis known as rhombomeres (r), which give rise to the cerebellum, pons, and medulla later on Ghosh and Sagerström, 2018; Parker and Krumlauf, 2020.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations (Ghosh and Sagerström, 2018; Parker and Krumlauf, 2020).

claim: Rhombomeres give rise to the cerebellum, pons, and medulla.
source: During vertebrate development, the hindbrain forms eight metameric segmented units along the antero-posterior (A-P) axis known as rhombomeres (r), which give rise to the cerebellum, pons, and medulla later on Ghosh and Sagerström, 2018; Parker and Krumlauf, 2020.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations (Ghosh and Sagerström, 2018; Parker and Krumlauf, 2020).

claim: Hox1-5 genes are expressed in a nested overlapping pattern with rhombomere-specific boundaries in the embryonic hindbrain.
source: In the embryonic hindbrain, Hox1-5 genes are expressed in a nested overlapping pattern with rhombomere-specific boundaries.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Hox gene expression patterns in the hindbrain.

claim: The Hox code is critical for the establishment of rhombomeric territories and the determination of cell fates.
source: This Hox code is critical for the establishment of rhombomeric territories and the determination of cell fates (Barsh et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2016; Parker and Krumlauf, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Barsh et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2016; Parker and Krumlauf, 2020).

claim: Hox genes play vital roles in neuronal migration and circuit formation at later embryonic stages.
source: At later embryonic stages, Hox genes also play vital roles in neuronal migration and circuit formation (Feng et al., 2021; Hockman et al., 2019; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Feng et al., 2021; Hockman et al., 2019; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2013).

claim: Pontine nuclei neurons originate at the posterior rhombic lip of r6-r8.
source: For example, neurons in the pontine nuclei (PN), which acts as an information integration station between the cortex and cerebellum (Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020), originate at the posterior rhombic lip of r6-r8, migrate tangentially to the rostral ventral hindbrain, and then receive different inputs from the cortex, in which the specific expression pattern of Hox3-5 genes determines the migration routines, cellular organization, and neuronal circuits (Geisen et al., 2008; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020; Di Meglio et al., 2013; Lizen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work describing PN neuron development.

claim: Pontine nuclei neurons migrate tangentially to the rostral ventral hindbrain.
source: For example, neurons in the pontine nuclei (PN), which acts as an information integration station between the cortex and cerebellum (Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020), originate at the posterior rhombic lip of r6-r8, migrate tangentially to the rostral ventral hindbrain, and then receive different inputs from the cortex, in which the specific expression pattern of Hox3-5 genes determines the migration routines, cellular organization, and neuronal circuits (Geisen et al., 2008; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020; Di Meglio et al., 2013; Lizen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work describing PN neuron development.

claim: The pontine nuclei act as an information integration station between the cortex and cerebellum.
source: For example, neurons in the pontine nuclei (PN), which acts as an information integration station between the cortex and cerebellum (Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020), originate at the posterior rhombic lip of r6-r8, migrate tangentially to the rostral ventral hindbrain, and then receive different inputs from the cortex, in which the specific expression pattern of Hox3-5 genes determines the migration routines, cellular organization, and neuronal circuits (Geisen et al., 2008; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020; Di Meglio et al., 2013; Lizen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020).

claim: The specific expression pattern of Hox3-5 genes determines the migration routines, cellular organization, and neuronal circuits of PN neurons.
source: For example, neurons in the pontine nuclei (PN), which acts as an information integration station between the cortex and cerebellum (Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020), originate at the posterior rhombic lip of r6-r8, migrate tangentially to the rostral ventral hindbrain, and then receive different inputs from the cortex, in which the specific expression pattern of Hox3-5 genes determines the migration routines, cellular organization, and neuronal circuits (Geisen et al., 2008; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020; Di Meglio et al., 2013; Lizen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Geisen et al., 2008; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020; Di Meglio et al., 2013; Lizen et al., 2017).

claim: Hox gene expression is maintained up to postnatal and even adult stages in the hindbrain derivatives.
source: Note that Hox gene expression is maintained up to postnatal and even adult stages in the hindbrain derivatives (Farago et al., 2006; Feng et al., 2021; Kratochwil et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Farago et al., 2006; Feng et al., 2021; Kratochwil et al., 2017).

claim: Hox pattern maintenance is generally governed by epigenetic regulators, especially the polycomb-group (PcG) and trithorax-group (trxG) complexes.
source: Hox pattern maintenance is generally governed by epigenetic regulators, especially the polycomb-group (PcG) and trithorax-group (trxG) complexes, which repress and activate Hox genes, respectively (Bahrampour et al., 2019; Chopra et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2022; Papp and Müller, 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations (Bahrampour et al., 2019; Chopra et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2022; Papp and Müller, 2006).

claim: PcG complexes repress Hox genes.
source: Hox pattern maintenance is generally governed by epigenetic regulators, especially the polycomb-group (PcG) and trithorax-group (trxG) complexes, which repress and activate Hox genes, respectively (Bahrampour et al., 2019; Chopra et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2022; Papp and Müller, 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TrxG complexes activate Hox genes.
source: Hox pattern maintenance is generally governed by epigenetic regulators, especially the polycomb-group (PcG) and trithorax-group (trxG) complexes, which repress and activate Hox genes, respectively (Bahrampour et al., 2019; Chopra et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2022; Papp and Müller, 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Different SET/MLL proteins and a common multi-subunit core module consisting of WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L, and DPY-30 (WRAD) constitute the COMPASS family of TrxG complexes in mammals.
source: In mammals, different SET/MLL proteins and a common multi-subunit core module consisting of WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L, and DPY-30 (WRAD) constitute the COMPASS (complex of proteins associated with Set1) family of TrxG complexes, which acts as a methyltransferase generally (Cenik and Shilatifard, 2021; Jambhekar et al., 2019; Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations (Cenik and Shilatifard, 2021; Jambhekar et al., 2019; Schuettengruber et al., 2017).

claim: The COMPASS family of TrxG complexes acts as a methyltransferase.
source: In mammals, different SET/MLL proteins and a common multi-subunit core module consisting of WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L, and DPY-30 (WRAD) constitute the COMPASS (complex of proteins associated with Set1) family of TrxG complexes, which acts as a methyltransferase generally (Cenik and Shilatifard, 2021; Jambhekar et al., 2019; Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations (Cenik and Shilatifard, 2021; Jambhekar et al., 2019; Schuettengruber et al., 2017).

claim: WDR5 plays a central scaffolding role in the COMPASS complex.
source: Among them, WDR5 plays a central scaffolding role and has been shown to act as a key regulator of Hox maintenance (Wang et al., 2011; Wysocka et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Wang et al., 2011; Wysocka et al., 2005).

claim: WDR5 has been shown to act as a key regulator of Hox maintenance.
source: Among them, WDR5 plays a central scaffolding role and has been shown to act as a key regulator of Hox maintenance (Wang et al., 2011; Wysocka et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Wang et al., 2011; Wysocka et al., 2005).

claim: WDR5 is responsible for MLL-mediated HOXA9 activation in acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: In acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia, WDR5 is responsible for MLL-mediated HOXA9 activation and is a potential drug target (Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021).

claim: WDR5 is a potential drug target in acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: In acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia, WDR5 is responsible for MLL-mediated HOXA9 activation and is a potential drug target (Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021).

claim: WDR5 facilitates HOTTIP to recruit the MLL complex and stimulate HOXA9 and HOXA13 expression during the progression of prostate and liver tumors.
source: In addition, WDR5 facilitates HOTTIP, a long noncoding RNA, to recruit the MLL complex and thus stimulate HOXA9 and HOXA13 expression during the progression of prostate and liver tumors (Fu et al., 2017; Malek et al., 2017; Quagliata et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Fu et al., 2017; Malek et al., 2017; Quagliata et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2020).

claim: Rnf220-/- mice are neonatal lethal.
source: Although our previous reports have shown that Rnf220-/- mice is neonatal lethal and the survived Rnf220+/- mice develop severe motor impairments, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood (Ma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Ma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019).

claim: Rnf220+/- mice develop severe motor impairments.
source: Although our previous reports have shown that Rnf220-/- mice is neonatal lethal and the survived Rnf220+/- mice develop severe motor impairments, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood (Ma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Ma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019).

claim: Several Hox genes were up-regulated in the mouse brain of both Rnf220+/- and Rnf220-/- genotypes at E18.5.
source: Based on microarray analysis, we explored changes in expression profiles in E18.5 Rnf220+/- and Rnf220-/- mouse brains, which breed floxed Rnf220 to Vasa-Cre mice. Interestingly, several Hox genes were up-regulated in the mouse brain of both genotypes (Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by microarray analysis data as indicated in Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: Hox gene up-regulation in Rnf220-deficient mice was observed only in late embryonic stages after E15.5.
source: Considering that Hox expression in forebrain is too low (data not shown), we focus on the hindbrain and found that this phenomenon was observed only in late embryonic stages after E15.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 comparing E15.5 and E16.5 timepoints.

claim: There is no significant difference in the upregulation of Hox genes between Rnf220+/- and Rnf220-/- mice.
source: Since Rnf220-/- mice is neonatal lethal and there is not significant difference in the upregulation of Hox genes between Rnf220+/- and Rnf220-/- mice, Rnf220+/- mice were used in subsequent assays in this study.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from both genotypes, leading to the decision to use Rnf220+/- mice for subsequent experiments.

claim: Both Hoxa9 and Hoxb9 were exclusively up-regulated in the brainstem of Rnf220+/- mice.
source: Notably, both Hoxa9 and Hoxb9 were exclusively up-regulated in the brainstem of Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D examining different CNS regions.

claim: The up-regulation of Hox genes was restricted to the pons in the Rnf220+/- mice.
source: Further, we confirmed that the up-regulation of Hox genes was restricted to the pons in the Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F examining different brainstem sections.

claim: RNA-seq analysis of the pons revealed an overall increase in Hox gene expression in adult Rnf220+/- mice.
source: In addition, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis of the pons also revealed an overall increase in Hox gene expression in adult Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the heatmap in Figure 1A.

claim: 15 cell clusters were identified by UMAP in both the WT and Rnf220+/- pons groups.
source: 15 cell clusters were identified by uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) in both the WT and Rnf220+/- groups (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq analysis and UMAP visualization shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Most of the cell clusters in the pons were identified as distinct neuronal groups.
source: When we annotate these cell clusters by their uniquely and highly expressed markers (Supplementary file 3), we found that most of the clusters were identified as distinct neuronal groups (cluster_1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, and 13), in addition to astrocyte (cluster_5), oligodendrocyte (cluster_3), oligodendrocyte precursor (cluster_14), ependymal cell (cluster_9), and a group not corresponding to any known cell types (cluster_0) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of marker gene expression patterns shown in Supplementary file 3 and Figure 1B.

claim: Up-regulation of Hox genes was most pronounced in three cell clusters (cluster_2, 7, and 10) in the Rnf220+/- pons.
source: Then, the Hox gene expression levels for each cell clusters were analyzed and found that up-regulation of Hox genes was most pronounced in three of these clusters (cluster_2, 7, and 10) (Figure 1D), albeit with distinct profiles.
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D displaying Hox expression across cell clusters.

claim: Hox7-10 genes were up-regulated in cluster_2.
source: Hox7-10 genes were up-regulated genes in cluster_2, while Hox3-5 and Hox1-3 genes were activated in cluster_7 and 10, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hox3-5 genes were activated in cluster_7.
source: Hox7-10 genes were up-regulated genes in cluster_2, while Hox3-5 and Hox1-3 genes were activated in cluster_7 and 10, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hox1-3 genes were activated in cluster_10.
source: Hox7-10 genes were up-regulated genes in cluster_2, while Hox3-5 and Hox1-3 genes were activated in cluster_7 and 10, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rnf220 knockdown further enhanced the activation of many Hox genes by RA in P19 cells.
source: Rnf220 knockdown further enhanced the activation of many Hox genes, including Hoxa1, Hoxb1, Hoxa9, and Hoxb9, by RA presence (Figure 1E), suggesting a general role of Rnf220 in Hox regulation.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Rnf220 knockdown had no clear effect on Hox expression in the absence of RA in P19 cells.
source: Note that Rnf220 knockdown had no clear effect on Hox expression in the absence of RA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Cluster_10 likely represents cells derived from rhombomeres 2-5.
source: When we refer to the transcriptomic profiles of each cluster in the pons, we found that the cluster_10 likely represents cells derived from rhombomeres 2–5, given their expression of endogenous anterior Hox genes (Hox1-3), while the cluster_7 likely represents cells derived from rhombomeres 6–8, as evidenced by the expression of Hox3-5 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of Hox1-3 genes in cluster_10 as shown in Figure 1D, based on known Hox expression patterns along the A-P axis.

claim: Cluster_7 likely represents cells derived from rhombomeres 6-8.
source: When we refer to the transcriptomic profiles of each cluster in the pons, we found that the cluster_10 likely represents cells derived from rhombomeres 2–5, given their expression of endogenous anterior Hox genes (Hox1-3), while the cluster_7 likely represents cells derived from rhombomeres 6–8, as evidenced by the expression of Hox3-5 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of Hox3-5 genes in cluster_7 as shown in Figure 1D, based on known Hox expression patterns along the A-P axis.

claim: PN-specific markers, including Nfib, Pax6, and Barhl1, were enriched in cluster_7.
source: After mapping known neuron-specific markers to each cluster, PN-specific markers, including Nfib, Pax6, and Barhl1, were enriched in the cluster_7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Some PN markers were up-regulated in Rnf220+/- mice compared to WT mice.
source: The quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) results showed that compared to WT mice, some PN markers were up-regulated in Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PN neurons serve as relay cells between the cerebral cortex and cerebellum.
source: Originating at the posterior rhombic lip and migrating tangentially to their final position in the ventral part of the pons, PN neurons serve as relay cells between the cerebral cortex and cerebellum (Di Meglio et al., 2013; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Di Meglio et al., 2013; Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020).

claim: The expression pattern of Hox genes is crucial for the migration and the final neuronal circuit formation of the PN neurons.
source: The expression pattern of Hox genes is crucial for the migration and the final neuronal circuit formation of the PN neurons (Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Kratochwil et al., 2017; Maheshwari et al., 2020).

claim: Hox4-5 expression levels were up-regulated in the Rnf220+/- PN.
source: The results of RT-PCR assays indicated an up-regulation in Hox4-5 expression levels in the Rnf220+/- PN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the PN, endogenous Hox3 is ubiquitously expressed throughout the PN.
source: In the PN, endogenous Hox3-5 genes exhibit a nested and unique expression pattern along the rostral-caudal axis, with Hox3 ubiquitously expressed throughout the PN, Hox4 localized to the middle and posterior regions, and Hox5 confined to the posterior segment (Kratochwil et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PN Hox expression patterns supported by citation (Kratochwil et al., 2017).

claim: In the PN, endogenous Hox4 is localized to the middle and posterior regions.
source: In the PN, endogenous Hox3-5 genes exhibit a nested and unique expression pattern along the rostral-caudal axis, with Hox3 ubiquitously expressed throughout the PN, Hox4 localized to the middle and posterior regions, and Hox5 confined to the posterior segment (Kratochwil et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PN Hox expression patterns supported by citation (Kratochwil et al., 2017).

claim: In the PN, endogenous Hox5 is confined to the posterior segment.
source: In the PN, endogenous Hox3-5 genes exhibit a nested and unique expression pattern along the rostral-caudal axis, with Hox3 ubiquitously expressed throughout the PN, Hox4 localized to the middle and posterior regions, and Hox5 confined to the posterior segment (Kratochwil et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PN Hox expression patterns supported by citation (Kratochwil et al., 2017).

claim: All the Hox3-5 paralogs were uniformly up-regulated along the rostral-caudal axis in the Rnf220+/- PN.
source: The results showed that all the Hox3-5 paralogs were uniformly up-regulated along the rostral-caudal axis in the Rnf220+/- PN (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A examining rostral, middle, and caudal PN sections.

claim: There is no difference in PN structure between WT and Rnf220+/- mice.
source: There is no difference of structure in PN or even pons between WT and Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B; Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by Nissl staining, DAPI labeling, and measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B, and Figure 2C-E.

claim: There is no difference in pons structure between WT and Rnf220+/- mice.
source: There is no difference of structure in PN or even pons between WT and Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B; Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by Nissl staining and DAPI labeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Fewer PN neurons were targeted by axons from the motor cortex in the Rnf220+/- mice.
source: The results showed that fewer PN neurons were targeted by axons from the motor cortex in the Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 2C and F–G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by neuronal tracing data shown in Figure 2C, F-G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The projection from the motor cortex was centralized in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice.
source: In addition, the projection from the motor cortex was centralized in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by neuronal tracing data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Down-regulated H3K27me3 signals were observed in some Hox clusters in hindbrain of Rnf220+/- mice.
source: Indeed, we did observe the local epigenetic modification changes, i.e., the down-regulated H3K27me3 signals and up-regulated H3K4me3 signals, in some Hox cluster in hindbrain of Rnf220+/- mice by ChIP-qPCR assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Up-regulated H3K4me3 signals were observed in some Hox clusters in hindbrain of Rnf220+/- mice.
source: Indeed, we did observe the local epigenetic modification changes, i.e., the down-regulated H3K27me3 signals and up-regulated H3K4me3 signals, in some Hox cluster in hindbrain of Rnf220+/- mice by ChIP-qPCR assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The protein levels of the core components of PcG examined were comparable between WT and Rnf220+/- mice.
source: Therefore, protein levels of the core components of PcG and TrxG complexes in the mouse hindbrain and pons were examined and the results showed that although the protein levels of the core components of PcG we examined were comparable between WT and Rnf220+/-, a clear increase in the protein level of WDR5, a key component of the trxG complex, was observed in the hindbrain of both Rnf220+/-and Rnf220-/- mouse embryos at E18.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B; Figure 3A), the phenomenon was also observed at E16.5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: A clear increase in the protein level of WDR5 was observed in the hindbrain of both Rnf220+/- and Rnf220-/- mouse embryos at E18.5.
source: Therefore, protein levels of the core components of PcG and TrxG complexes in the mouse hindbrain and pons were examined and the results showed that although the protein levels of the core components of PcG we examined were comparable between WT and Rnf220+/-, a clear increase in the protein level of WDR5, a key component of the trxG complex, was observed in the hindbrain of both Rnf220+/-and Rnf220-/- mouse embryos at E18.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B; Figure 3A), the phenomenon was also observed at E16.5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The increase in WDR5 protein level in Rnf220-deficient mice was also observed at E16.5.
source: Therefore, protein levels of the core components of PcG and TrxG complexes in the mouse hindbrain and pons were examined and the results showed that although the protein levels of the core components of PcG we examined were comparable between WT and Rnf220+/-, a clear increase in the protein level of WDR5, a key component of the trxG complex, was observed in the hindbrain of both Rnf220+/-and Rnf220-/- mouse embryos at E18.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B; Figure 3A), the phenomenon was also observed at E16.5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The increase in the protein level of WDR5 was only observed in the pons, but not in the cortex or cerebellum, in Rnf220+/- mice.
source: We next tested the expression of WDR5 in the mouse pons, cortex, and cerebellum at adult and found that the increase in the protein level of WDR5 was only observed in the pons, but not in the cortex or cerebellum, in Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 3C and E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D), which is consistent with the pons-specific up-regulation in Hox genes expression.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C, E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The protein level of WDR5 was enhanced in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice.
source: In addition, the protein level of WDR5 was also enhanced in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 3D) and Rnf220 knockdown P19 cells in the presence of RA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The protein level of WDR5 was enhanced in Rnf220 knockdown P19 cells in the presence of RA.
source: In addition, the protein level of WDR5 was also enhanced in the PN of Rnf220+/- mice (Figure 3D) and Rnf220 knockdown P19 cells in the presence of RA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: WDR5 co-immunoprecipitated with RNF220 in HEK293 cells.
source: Indeed, in HEK293 cells transiently co-transfected with FLAG-tagged RNF220 and myc-tagged WDR5, WDR5 co-immunoprecipitated with RNF220 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RNF220 co-immunoprecipitated with WDR5 in HEK293 cells.
source: In the reverse experiment, RNF220 also co-immunoprecipitated with WDR5 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Endogenous RNF220 co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous WDR5 in the brainstem.
source: Furthermore, in the brainstem, when WDR5 was immunoprecipitated using an anti-WDR5 antibody, endogenous RNF220 was also detected in the immunoprecipitate.
evidence: This is supported by endogenous co-immunoprecipitation data as described in the text and likely shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Co-expression of WT RNF220 clearly reduced the protein level of WDR5 in HEK293 cells.
source: The results showed that co-expression of WT RNF220, but not the ligase-dead mutant (W539A) or the RING domain deletion (△Ring) form, clearly reduced the protein level of WDR5 in HEK293 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The ligase-dead mutant (W539A) RNF220 did not reduce the protein level of WDR5 in HEK293 cells.
source: The results showed that co-expression of WT RNF220, but not the ligase-dead mutant (W539A) or the RING domain deletion (△Ring) form, clearly reduced the protein level of WDR5 in HEK293 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The RING domain deletion (△Ring) form of RNF220 did not reduce the protein level of WDR5 in HEK293 cells.
source: The results showed that co-expression of WT RNF220, but not the ligase-dead mutant (W539A) or the RING domain deletion (△Ring) form, clearly reduced the protein level of WDR5 in HEK293 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The reduction in the protein level of WDR5 by RNF220 overexpression was blocked by MG132.
source: In addition, the reduction in the protein level of WDR5 by RNF220 overexpression was blocked by MG132, suggesting a role for the proteasome in this regulation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E demonstrating rescue of WDR5 levels by proteasome inhibitor MG132.

claim: Co-expression of RNF220 strongly enhanced the polyubiquitination of WDR5 protein.
source: It was found that co-expression of RNF220 strongly enhanced the polyubiquitination of WDR5 protein, and this regulation depends on the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of RNF220 because RNF220△Ring failed to promote the polyubiquitination of WDR5 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: RNF220-mediated polyubiquitination of WDR5 depends on the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of RNF220.
source: It was found that co-expression of RNF220 strongly enhanced the polyubiquitination of WDR5 protein, and this regulation depends on the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of RNF220 because RNF220△Ring failed to promote the polyubiquitination of WDR5 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4F comparing WT and △Ring RNF220.

claim: The polyubiquitination level of endogenous WDR5 in Rnf220+/- mouse pons was markedly decreased compared to WT mice.
source: Moreover, when the endogenous WDR5 protein was immunoprecipitated from the mouse pons, its polyubiquitination level in Rnf220+/- mice was markedly decreased compared to WT mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: WDR5 was only ubiquitinated by RNF220 when K48-type ubiquitin was present.
source: Indeed, WDR5 were only ubiquitinated by RNF220 when K48-type ubiquitin was present (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4H using different ubiquitin mutants.

claim: When the K48R mutated ubiquitin was co-expressed, the RNF220-induced polyubiquitination level of WDR5 protein was fully diminished.
source: Consistent with this, when the K48R mutated ubiquitin was co-expressed, the RNF220-induced polyubiquitination level of WDR5 protein was fully diminished (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The WDR5 truncate remaining 1-127aa was sufficient to be degraded by RNF220.
source: To determine the exact lysines ubiquitinated by RNF220, we first tested the effects of RNF220 on the stability of different WDR5 truncates and found that the truncate remaining 1-127aa was enough to be degraded by RNF220, suggesting the corresponding lysines were included in this region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A testing different WDR5 truncates.

claim: K109, K112, and K120 in WDR5 were required for the polyubiquitination of WDR5 by RNF220.
source: We individually mutated all these conserved lysines into arginines and then examined RNF220-mediated ubiquitination of each mutant. It was found that K109, K112, and K120 were required for the polyubiquitination of WDR5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B testing individual lysine mutations.

claim: When K109, K112, and K120 were simultaneously mutated into arginines, RNF220 failed to enhance the polyubiquitination levels of the resulted WDR5-3KR mutants.
source: Furthermore, when these lysine residues were simultaneously mutated into arginines, RNF220 failed to enhance the polyubiquitination levels of the resulted WDR5-3KR mutants (Figure 4I), suggesting that these lysine residues are direct ubiquitination sites.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4I testing the triple lysine mutant.

claim: K109, K112, and K120 in WDR5 are direct ubiquitination sites for RNF220.
source: Furthermore, when these lysine residues were simultaneously mutated into arginines, RNF220 failed to enhance the polyubiquitination levels of the resulted WDR5-3KR mutants (Figure 4I), suggesting that these lysine residues are direct ubiquitination sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of ubiquitination when these lysines are mutated, as shown in Figure 4I.

claim: RNF220 regulates WDR5 ubiquitination by adding K48-linked polyubiquitin chains at the lysine sites of K109, K112, and K120.
source: Together, these results indicate that RNF220 regulates WDR5 ubiquitination by adding K48-linked polyubiquitin chains at the lysine sites of K109, K112, and K120.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 4F-I demonstrating K48-linkage specificity and identification of specific lysine residues.

claim: The stimulation of Hox genes by Rnf220 knockdown was significantly reduced when Wdr5 was knocked down simultaneously in P19 cells in the presence of RA.
source: It is observed that the stimulation of Hox genes by Rnf220 knockdown was significantly reduced when Wdr5 was knocked down simultaneously by small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) in the presence of RA (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A-C demonstrating rescue of Hox expression by Wdr5 knockdown.

claim: The expression levels of Hox genes showed no clear changes when without RA in P19 cells with Rnf220 and Wdr5 knockdown.
source: Note that the expression levels of Hox genes showed no clear changes when without RA or only Wdr5 was knocked down in P19 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The expression levels of Hox genes showed no clear changes when only Wdr5 was knocked down in P19 cells.
source: Note that the expression levels of Hox genes showed no clear changes when without RA or only Wdr5 was knocked down in P19 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The up-regulation of Hox3-5 genes in the hindbrain of Rnf220+/- embryos was largely reversed by WDR5-IN-4.
source: It was found that the up-regulation of Hox3-5 genes in the hindbrain of the Rnf220+/- embryos was largely reversed by WDR5-IN-4 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C following in utero injection of WDR5 inhibitor.

claim: WDR5-IN-4 injection had no effect on the endogenous Rnf220 expression in the hindbrain.
source: Notably, we found that WDR5-IN-4 injection had no effect on the endogenous Rnf220 expression in the hindbrain (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The up-regulation of Hox3-5 genes in the pons of Rnf220fl/wt;Nestin-Cre mice were markedly recovered by Wdr5 genetic ablation in Rnf220fl/wt;Wdr5fl/wt;Nestin-Cre mice.
source: It was found that the up-regulation of Hox3-5 genes in the pons of Rnf220fl/wt;Nestin-Cre mice were markedly recovered by Wdr5 genetic ablation in Rnf220fl/wt;Wdr5fl/wt;Nestin-Cre mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E comparing different genetic combinations.

claim: H3K27me3 was up-regulated in Rnf220 and Wdr5 double knockdown P19 cell line related to Rnf220 single knockdown P19 cell line in the presence of RA.
source: ChIP-qPCR also showed the local epigenetic modification changes in some Hox cluster, with H3K27me3 up-regulated and H3K4me3 down-regulated in Rnf220 and Wdr5 double knockdown P19 cell line related to Rnf220 single knockdown P19 cell line in the presence of RA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3K4me3 was down-regulated in Rnf220 and Wdr5 double knockdown P19 cell line related to Rnf220 single knockdown P19 cell line in the presence of RA.
source: ChIP-qPCR also showed the local epigenetic modification changes in some Hox cluster, with H3K27me3 up-regulated and H3K4me3 down-regulated in Rnf220 and Wdr5 double knockdown P19 cell line related to Rnf220 single knockdown P19 cell line in the presence of RA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rnf220 deficiency induces the up-regulation of Hox genes in the mouse hindbrain.
source: Taken together, Rnf220 dificiency induces the up-regulation of Hox genes in the mouse hindbrain and thus a defects in cortex-PN nueronal circuits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Rnf220 deficiency causes defects in cortex-PN neuronal circuits.
source: Taken together, Rnf220 dificiency induces the up-regulation of Hox genes in the mouse hindbrain and thus a defects in cortex-PN nueronal circuits.
evidence: This is supported by neuronal tracing data shown in Figure 2 demonstrating altered projection patterns.

claim: RNF220 regulates the protein stability of WDR5 via ubiquitination in the mouse hindbrain.
source: Mechanistically, we found that RNF220 regulates the protein stability of WDR5 via ubiquitination in the mouse hindbrain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4 demonstrating protein-protein interaction, ubiquitination, and degradation.

claim: WDR5 conditional knockdown reversed the up-regulation of Hox genes expression in Rnf220 deficient mice.
source: WDR5 conditional knockdown or functional inhibition reversed the up-regulation of Hox genes expression in Rnf220 deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E demonstrating rescue in genetic ablation experiments.

claim: WDR5 functional inhibition reversed the up-regulation of Hox genes expression in Rnf220 deficient mice.
source: WDR5 conditional knockdown or functional inhibition reversed the up-regulation of Hox genes expression in Rnf220 deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C demonstrating rescue by WDR5-IN-4 inhibitor.

claim: The regulation of WDR5 by RNF220 is involved in the maintenance of Hox expression pattern in the mouse hindbrain.
source: The above findings support the involvement of WDR5 regulation by RNF220 in the maintenance of Hox expression pattern in the mouse hindbrain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the rescue experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Hox genes play key roles in the regulation of synapse formation, neuronal terminal identity, and neural circuit assembly at late developmental stages.
source: In addition to their roles in progenitor cell specification, cell survival, neuronal migration, axon guidance, and dendrite morphogenesis during early development stages (Smith and Kratsios, 2024), Hox genes also play key roles in the regulation of synapse formation, neuronal terminal identity, and neural circuit assembly at late stages (Feng et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2021; Philippidou and Dasen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Feng et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2021; Philippidou and Dasen, 2013).

claim: RNF220 and WDR5 have a dose-dependent role in the maintenance of Hox expression in the hindbrain.
source: Our study revealed a dose-dependent role of RNF220 and WDR5 in the maintenance of Hox expression in the hindbrain, which might have a functional role in the neural circuit organization of the pons in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Rnf220+/- and Rnf220-/- mice show Hox upregulation, and rescue experiments with partial Wdr5 reduction are effective.

claim: WDR5 has been reported to be absolutely required for the regulation of Hox genes expression during mammalian embryo development.
source: In mammals, WDR5, a key component of the COMPASS-related complexes, has been reported to be absolutely required for the regulation of Hox genes expression during mammalian embryo development and cancer progression via different mechanisms (Wysocka et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Wysocka et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021).

claim: WDR5 has been reported to be absolutely required for the regulation of Hox genes expression during cancer progression.
source: In mammals, WDR5, a key component of the COMPASS-related complexes, has been reported to be absolutely required for the regulation of Hox genes expression during mammalian embryo development and cancer progression via different mechanisms (Wysocka et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Wysocka et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021).

claim: The stabilization of WDR5 upon RNF220 knockdown was recapitulated in RA-treated P19 cells.
source: The stabilization of WDR5 and stimulation of Hox expression upon RNF220 knockdown was also recapitulated in RA-treated P19 cells, a cellular model for Hox regulation study.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The stimulation of Hox expression upon RNF220 knockdown was recapitulated in RA-treated P19 cells.
source: The stabilization of WDR5 and stimulation of Hox expression upon RNF220 knockdown was also recapitulated in RA-treated P19 cells, a cellular model for Hox regulation study.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Different Hox stimulation profiles were detected in different neuronal groups at single cell level.
source: Interestingly, when examined at single cell level, different Hox stimulation profiles were detected in different neuronal groups, so that Hox1-3 were up-regulated in cluster 10, while Hox3-5 and Hox7-10 up-regulation appeared in cluster 7 and cluster 2, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cluster 2 was defined as glycinergic neuron cells by specific Slc6a5 expression.
source: Cluster 2 is most interesting in that, Hox7-10 were up-regulated in these cells which were not expressed in WT hindbrain. This cluster was defined as glycinergic neuron cells by specific Slc6a5 expression.
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis from snRNA-seq data.

claim: The regulation of WDR5 and Hox expression by RNF220 is context dependent and precisely controlled in vivo.
source: The regulation of WDR5 and Hox expression by RNF220 seems to be context dependent and precisely controlled in vivo, depending on the molecular and epigenetic status of the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WDR5 levels are only affected in specific brain regions (pons) and under specific conditions (RA treatment in P19 cells).

claim: WDR5 levels are not affected in most regions in the Rnf220+/- brain, including the cortex and cerebellum.
source: For example, although WDR5 and RNF220 are widely co-expressed in the brain, WDR5 levels are not affected in most regions in the Rnf220+/- brain, including the cortex, cerebellum, etc. (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: EED is targeted by RNF220 in the cerebellum, but not in the pons.
source: This is also true for EED, another epigenetic regulator, which is targeted by RNF220 in the cerebellum, but not in the pons (Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Ma et al., 2020).

claim: In untreated P19 cells, knockdown of RNF220 has no effect on the stability of endogenous WDR5.
source: In untreated P19 cells, knockdown of RNF220 also has no effect on the stability of endogenous WDR5, although overexpression of RNF220 did reduce WDR5 level in 293T cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F comparing conditions with and without RA.

claim: Overexpression of RNF220 reduced WDR5 level in 293T cells.
source: In untreated P19 cells, knockdown of RNF220 also has no effect on the stability of endogenous WDR5, although overexpression of RNF220 did reduce WDR5 level in 293T cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: RA treatment of P19 cells helps to set up the molecular environment that facilitates Hox expression as well as RNF220-WDR5 interaction.
source: We suggest that RA treatment of P19 cells helps to set up the molecular environment that facilitates Hox expression as well as RNF220-WDR5 interaction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that RNF220-WDR5 regulation is only evident in RA-treated P19 cells.

claim: WDR5 is a RNF220 target involved in the maintenance of Hox expression and development of the pons.
source: In summary, our data support WDR5 as a RNF220 target involved in the maintenance of Hox expression and thus development of the pons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rnf220 is strongly expressed in the embryonic mouse mid/hindbrain.
source: Rnf220 is strongly expressed in the embryonic mouse mid/hindbrain (Ma et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Ma et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022).

claim: Rnf220 floxed mice were originally 129Sz/SvPasCrl background and mated with C57BL/6.
source: Rnf220 floxed mice (Rnf220fl/fl) were originally 129Sz/SvPasCrl background and mated with C57BL/6 then.
evidence: This describes the genetic background of the mouse strains used in the study.

claim: Vasa-Cre mice were used to mate with Rnf220 floxed mice to generate Rnf220 germ cell knockout or heterozygote mice.
source: Vasa-Cre mice were used to mate with Rnf220 floxed mice (Rnf220fl/fl) to generate Rnf220 germ cell knockout (Rnf220-/-) or heterozygote (Rnf220+/-) mice.
evidence: This describes the breeding strategy used to generate the experimental mice.

claim: Nestin-Cre mice were used to mate with Rnf220fl/fl and Wdr5 floxed mice to generate conditional neural specific knockout or heterozygote mice.
source: Nestin-Cre mice were used to mate with Rnf220fl/fl and Wdr5 floxed mice (Wdr5fl/fl) to generate conditional neural specific knockout or heterozygote mice.
evidence: This describes the breeding strategy used to generate conditional knockout mice.

claim: In total, 125,956 and 122,266 cell transcriptomes were analyzed for WT and Rnf220+/- pons respectively in snRNA-seq analysis.
source: After filtering, a total of 125,956 and 122,266 cells for WT and Rnf220+/- pons respectively remained for subsequent analysis.
evidence: This describes the number of cells analyzed in the snRNA-seq experiment.
